c.tagline: Where the Hajar Mountains meet the Arabian Sea.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare with the driver before the ride, or use Careem for a set upfront price.

emergency.note: 9999 is the single nationwide number for police, ambulance and fire in Oman.

hood_landmark.Al Bustan / Bandar Jissah: Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel

avoid.reason: Crime is rare; agree taxi fares in advance and stay out of wadi beds during rain due to flash floods.

hood_desc: Muscat's historic old town: a working port, the atmospheric Mutrah Souq and a curving corniche lined with traditional dhow harbors and the fish market; suits culture-focused travelers and photographers who don't mind being away from the beach.

Muscat's beachfront resort strip lined with 5-star hotels, foreign embassies and upscale seafront dining; ideal for leisure travelers, couples and honeymooners who want sea views and a walkable promenade.
A leafy, expat-heavy commercial hub with Qurum Natural Park, shopping malls and a public beach; a practical, well-connected base for families and mid-range travelers who want amenities close by.

The bustling commercial downtown (CBD) with banks, the Ruwi souq ("Gold Souq") and the largest concentration of budget hotels; suits business travelers and backpackers who prioritize cost and transit links over scenery.

A secluded resort enclave in coves between the Hajar Mountains and the Gulf of Oman, east of the city center; best for luxury travelers and honeymooners seeking seclusion, though a car or taxi is needed for sightseeing.
lodging: Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel

water.note: Desalinated tap water meets international standards, though bottled water is widely preferred for taste.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver in small OMR denominations, or via the Mwasalat mobile app/prepaid card on some routes; exact change is helpful as buses rarely give change for large notes.
transit.hours: Most routes operate roughly 6:00am-10:00pm; there is minimal to no late-night service, so taxis or ride-hailing apps are needed after hours.
transit.note: Coverage and frequency are limited compared to other Gulf capitals; most residents and visitors rely on taxis, ride-hailing (Careem) or rental cars rather than the bus network.

bus: Mwasalat intercity coaches to Salalah, Sohar, Nizwa and Sur
ferry: National Ferries Company routes from Muscat to Khasab (Musandam)

airport.name: Muscat International Airport (MCT)
airport.drive: 30-40 min to Qurum/CBD; 45-60 min to Muttrah or Old Muscat depending on traffic

transit.m: Mwasalat Route 111 Airport Express bus (~45 min)
Official airport taxi counter (fixed pre-paid fare)

tip.r: Not deeply rooted in local custom; rounding up taxi fares and 5-10% at tourist-oriented restaurants is appreciated but never demanded.

food.name: Shuwa
food.desc: Marinated lamb or camel wrapped in banana leaf, buried in a coal-filled pit and cooked for one to two days. Smoky, falling apart, festival food.

places.name: Ubhar
places.note: Muscat's leading contemporary Omani kitchen; slow-roasted camel shuwa is its signature.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Historic favourite in a restored merchant house above the corniche.

places.name: Ofair Omani Restaurant
places.note: Private curtained rooms with floor cushions; the shuwa is what locals order.

food.name: Majboos
food.desc: Oman's spiced rice plate, cooked with chicken, lamb or fish, saffron, dried lime and cardamom, and served on a shared platter.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Traditional menu in an atmospheric setting overlooking the harbour.

places.name: Ubhar
places.note: Refined version of the national rice dish, well-signposted for first-timers.

places.name: Kargeen Caffe
places.note: Garden restaurant under lanterns and trees; a long-time Muscat favourite.

food.name: Halwa Omani
food.desc: A dense amber jelly of starch, sugar, rosewater, saffron and nuts, stirred for hours in a copper vat. Offered to every guest with coffee.

places.name: Mutrah Souq halwa shops
places.note: Several shops in the souq sell it by the tub and hand out spoonfuls to taste.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Serves halwa the traditional way, with kahwa at the end of the meal.

places.name: Ubhar
places.note: Turns halwa into modern desserts and pastries as well as the classic form.

food.name: Mashuai
food.desc: Whole kingfish rubbed with spices, roasted over coals and served on lemon rice. The coastal centrepiece of an Omani feast.

places.name: Ubhar
places.note: Contemporary plating of the classic roast kingfish with lemon rice.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Seafood-strong Omani menu a few steps from the fish landing.

places.name: Mutrah Fish Market
places.note: Morning auction hall; nearby kitchens will grill what you buy.

food.name: Harees
food.desc: Wheat and meat cooked down and beaten to a smooth, savoury porridge, finished with ghee. Ramadan staple and comfort food year-round.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Keeps the older slow dishes on the menu alongside shuwa and majboos.

places.name: Ubhar
places.note: Serves harees as part of its Omani heritage selection.

places.name: Omani Heritage Restaurant
places.note: Straightforward local kitchen in the commercial district, popular at lunch.

food.name: Mishkak
food.desc: Skewers of beef, chicken or liver marinated in a tamarind and spice paste and grilled on roadside braziers after dark. Oman's street snack.

places.name: Mutrah Corniche stalls
places.note: Evening grills set up along the seafront once the heat drops.

places.name: Qurum Beach stalls
places.note: Weekend braziers beside the beach park, busy with Omani families.

places.name: Kargeen Caffe
places.note: Sit-down version of the street skewer in a shaded garden.

food.name: Omani kahwa
food.desc: Pale coffee brewed with cardamom and often rosewater, poured from a brass dallah into tiny cups and always served with dates or halwa.

places.name: Kargeen Caffe
places.note: Lantern-lit garden built for long coffee sessions with dates and shisha.

places.name: Bait Al Luban
places.note: Kahwa poured the traditional way to close the meal.

places.name: Mutrah Souq coffee stalls
places.note: Souq traders offer kahwa freely; frankincense and cardamom sold alongside.

food.name: Lemon-mint and laban
food.desc: Blitzed lemon with mint over crushed ice is the standard hot-weather order; salted laban buttermilk is the traditional partner to a rice plate.

places.name: Ruwi juice shops
places.note: Cheap, fast juice counters across the old commercial quarter.

places.name: Kargeen Caffe
places.note: Long list of fresh juices and laban served in the garden.

places.name: Mutrah Corniche cafes
places.note: Seafront cafes pouring lemon-mint by the jug at sunset.

landmarks: Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque
Oman's largest mosque, a breathtaking complex of white marble, intricate tilework, and one of the world's largest hand-woven carpets.
Al Alam Palace
The ceremonial palace of the Sultan of Oman, striking for its blue-and-gold pillared facade set between two historic forts.
Mutrah Corniche
A picturesque waterfront promenade lined with traditional dhows, whitewashed buildings, and mountain backdrops, especially stunning at sunset.
Royal Opera House Muscat
An architectural masterpiece blending Omani heritage with world-class design, a cultural centerpiece of the capital.
Mutrah Souq
One of the oldest marketplaces in the Arab world, a labyrinth of lantern-lit alleys selling frankincense, spices, and silver.
Al Jalali Fort
A 16th-century Portuguese-built fortress perched dramatically on rocks overlooking Muscat's harbor, an unmistakable symbol of the city.
Riyam Park Incense Burner Monument
A giant sculpture shaped like a traditional Omani incense burner (mabkhara) perched on a hilltop, offering sweeping views of the coastline.
Bait Al Zubair Museum
A beautifully curated museum in a traditional house showcasing Omani heritage, weaponry, and jewelry through the ages.
Qurum Beach
A relaxed, palm-fringed public beach popular with locals and visitors for its calm waters and skyline backdrop.
Muscat Gate Museum
A monumental ceremonial gate marking the entrance to Old Muscat, showcasing the city's fortified heritage.

train.note: Oman has no passenger railway - there are no intercity trains anywhere in the country in 2026 (a national/GCC network is still only planned). Long-distance travel is by road, coach or domestic ferry.

bus.note: Oman's national operator Mwasalat runs a daily air-conditioned Muscat-Dubai coach; it crosses the Hatta/Al Wajajah border, so bring your passport and check UAE/Oman visa rules. Mwasalat also runs the domestic intercity network from the Ruwi/Azaiba bus stations.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries run from Muscat. The National Ferries Company (nfconline.om) operates fast domestic coastal ferries, mainly Shinas-Khasab (Musandam), plus Shannah-Masirah Island - useful for getting around Oman but not for leaving the country.

half.name: Nizwa
half.blurb: Oman's old capital charms with a round fort, lively souq and date plantations.

half.name: Wadi Shab & Bimmah Sinkhole
half.blurb: Turquoise pools and a hidden waterfall reward a scenic canyon hike near the coast.

half.name: Wahiba Sands
half.blurb: Rolling golden dunes offer dune-bashing, camel rides and glorious desert sunsets.

half.name: Daymaniyat Islands
half.blurb: A protected island reserve with pristine reefs prized for snorkeling and diving.

full.name: Jebel Shams
full.blurb: Oman's highest peak overlooks a dramatic canyon nicknamed the Grand Canyon of Arabia.

full.name: Jebel Akhdar
full.blurb: A cool green mountain famed for terraced rose gardens and sweeping valley views.
